Dry days were strongly related to the number of light (10–25 mm) and average (26–50 mm) wet days.
With a one-year lead time, EGPR and bagged trees both reached a mean R² of 0.78, with EGPR having lower errors.
Removing individual input stations mostly had little effect, though Sylhet and Dinajpur were influential for some target stations.
The EGPR model stayed stable when one or two input stations were filled with random noise up to a coefficient of variation of 0.1.
relevance: Knowing in advance how dry the coming months are likely to be helps farmers choose crops and schedule irrigation, and helps authorities prepare for dry spells. The approach needs only rain gauge records, so it could be applied in other monsoon regions, including Korea, where seasonal dryness affects agriculture and water supply.

title: Use of basin outlet velocity to determine the basin concentration time and storage coefficient
authors: Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*

figure.caption: Events at one gauging station in the Chungju Dam basin: as the peak flow velocity rises, both the concentration time (a) and the storage coefficient (b) shrink, while the two parameters stay in a straight-line relation (c). Darker dots mark larger floods.
figure.credit: Figure 3 from Lee and Yoo (2022), Hydrology Research, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: The faster water flows at a basin outlet during a flood, the quicker the basin responds, and the study shows that this single velocity can be used to set both key unit-hydrograph parameters because their ratio stays fixed for a given basin.
background: Flood design in Korea relies on the Clark unit hydrograph, which needs two parameters: the concentration time (how long water takes to travel from the farthest point to the outlet) and the storage coefficient (how much the basin delays and damps the flow). Empirical formulas give typical values for ordinary floods, but in very large floods water moves faster and the basin reacts more quickly. Using ordinary-condition values for extreme design floods can therefore underestimate peak flows at major hydraulic structures.
approach: The authors first reviewed the theory linking concentration time to flow velocity and the storage coefficient to concentration time. They then analysed hourly rainfall and runoff from 1979 to 2018 at 21 water-level stations in the Chungju Dam basin (6,648 km²), using 57 rain gauges and observed peak velocities for 162 rainfall events of 30 mm or more. For each event, the two Clark parameters were estimated from the observed hydrograph, and their relationships with peak velocity were fitted and tested statistically. Finally, the basin was treated as ungauged and the parameters were rebuilt from peak velocity alone, then compared with the observed ones.
findings: Both the concentration time and the storage coefficient decreased as peak velocity increased, following a near-inverse relationship; at one station the fitted travel distance (84.5 km) was close to the actual channel length (90.3 km).
The storage coefficient was linearly proportional to the concentration time at every station (R² of 0.93 or higher), with ratios between 0.8 and 1.6 that tended to be larger in bigger basins.
A hypothesis test found no significant trend in this ratio with peak velocity at any station, so the ratio can be treated as a fixed basin characteristic regardless of event size.

Parameters derived from peak velocity alone differed from the observed ones by about 10% (concentration time) and 13% (storage coefficient) on average, and the resulting peak discharges and peak times differed by only 1.7% on average.
In larger basins the velocity-based method tended to overestimate the parameters, which leads to slightly low peak-flow estimates; dividing large basins into sub-basins could reduce this.
relevance: Dams, levees and bridges are designed for rare, extreme floods, when rivers run much faster than usual. This study offers a simple, physically based way to adjust flood-response parameters for those conditions using a single measurable quantity, the flow velocity at the outlet. It gives Korean engineers and water managers a practical check on formulas that were built for ordinary floods, and it points to estimating design-flood velocity in ungauged basins as the next challenge.

title: Extension methods of non-stationary time series based on wavelet analysis
authors: Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation

figure.caption: The three ways of resampling a wavelet spectrum: blocks of different length at each scale (Method 1), equal-length blocks drawn independently at each scale (Method 2), and equal-length blocks drawn at the same time for all scales (Method 3).
figure.credit: Figure 2 from Lee and Yoo (2022), Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation, CC BY-NC 4.0.

tldr: Resampling a series' wavelet spectrum in time blocks that keep all scales together, then transforming it back, produces long synthetic records that preserve both the original distribution and the co-movement between two series.
background: Climate and hydrological records are usually too short to capture long-term variability, so synthetic extensions are often generated. Classic tools such as ARMA models assume stationarity, while many climate-related series are non-stationary or quasi-periodic. Wavelet analysis captures how periodic behaviour changes over time and offers a way to build longer series that keep these features.
approach: The authors applied a continuous Morlet wavelet transform to a series, extended its spectrum by block resampling, and rebuilt a time series with the inverse transform. Three variants were compared: scale-dependent block lengths (Method 1), one block length for all scales sampled independently (Method 2), and one block length with the same time block drawn for all scales (Method 3). Block lengths came from the correlation length of the spectrum at each scale (up to about 114 months, roughly 9.5 years). The methods were tested on two synthetic non-stationary series of 672 months from nonlinear moving-average (NMA) and nonlinear autoregressive (NAR) models, extended to five times their length, and checked with box plots, bivariate wavelet analysis and 5,000 random realisations.
findings: All three methods produced extended spectra and series that looked broadly like the originals, but Method 1 left the spectrum fragmented at small scales.
Methods 1 and 2 squeezed values toward the median and missed the largest and smallest values, because drawing different times at different scales breaks the links between scales.

Method 3 reproduced the original distribution best, and its wavelet coherence showed that the co-movement between the two series was kept; the gap between methods was larger for the more skewed NMA series.
Phase (lead–lag) relationships between the two series were not preserved, and periods longer than the original record cannot be reproduced.
relevance: Water planners often need long, realistic climate or flow sequences to test reservoirs and drought plans, but observed records are short. This work shows a practical way to stretch records while keeping their changing cycles, and it highlights that relationships across time scales must be preserved to get realistic extremes.

title: Adequacy of the GK-2A AMI land surface temperature product according to geographic factors and compared with other satellite products (MODIS and S-VIRRS)
authors: Baik, J., Park, J., Jun, C., & Lee, J.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation

figure.caption: Number of days with valid observations (top) and the resulting 2020 annual mean land surface temperature (bottom) for S-VISSR, MODIS and GK-2A AMI over Korea; the polar-orbiting MODIS sees far fewer days and gives a much warmer annual mean.
figure.credit: Figure 6 from Baik et al. (2022), Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation, CC BY-NC 4.0.

tldr: Korea's geostationary satellite GK-2A estimated land surface temperature more accurately than MODIS and China's FY-2H S-VISSR at 106 ground stations, though it still runs a few degrees cold and loses accuracy at higher elevations.
background: Land surface temperature drives energy and water exchange between the ground and the air and is used for evapotranspiration, heat-wave and urban heat island studies. Ground stations are sparse, so satellites fill the gaps, but most validation work has focused on polar-orbiting sensors. The GEO-KOMPSAT-2A (GK-2A) satellite, launched in 2018, provides temperature every 10 minutes at 2 km resolution but had not been widely checked.
approach: Daily GK-2A AMI land surface temperature for 2020 was compared with ground measurements at 95 ASOS and 11 agricultural (AAOS) stations, and with two other products: MODIS/Terra MOD11A1 (polar orbit, 1 km) and FY-2H S-VISSR (geostationary, 5 km). Stations were grouped as inland (73) or coastal (33, within 5 km of the coast) and by elevation in 100 m bands. Bias, MAE, RMSE, relative RMSE and correlation were computed, and annual mean maps and observation counts were compared.
findings: All satellites followed the seasonal cycle, but GK-2A had the smallest errors: bias −3.12 °C inland and −2.70 °C on the coast, RMSE 4.85 and 4.49 °C, and correlation 0.94 and 0.91.
MODIS overestimated inland (bias +4.62 °C) and underestimated on the coast (−3.50 °C), while S-VISSR had the largest RMSE (6.31 and 5.61 °C) and covered only 20 of 33 coastal sites.

GK-2A underestimated most from April to September (−5.28 to −3.64 °C), when clouds and rain are frequent, and its RMSE rose with elevation (4.52–5.71 °C), about 1 °C worse at high sites than in lowlands.

Geostationary sensors had valid data on far more days (about 339 for AMI and 301 for S-VISSR versus about 125 for MODIS); MODIS's few clear-sky days pushed its annual mean to about 20.45 °C versus 7.29 °C for AMI and 8.27 °C for S-VISSR.
Annual mean maps clearly showed warmer urban areas such as Seoul, Daejeon, Daegu, Gwangju and Busan.
relevance: Reliable, frequent surface temperature maps help track heat waves and urban heat islands that affect public health and energy use in Korean cities. The study shows that Korea's own satellite is a strong option for this, while pointing out the coastal and terrain corrections still needed.

title: Estimation of grid-type precipitation quantile using satellite based re-analysis precipitation data in Korean peninsula
authors: Lee, J., Jun, C., Kim, H. J., Byun, J., & Baik, J.*
journal: Journal of Korea Water Resources Association

figure.caption: Percent difference between satellite-based (PERSIANN-CCS-CDR) and gauge-based (ASOS) design rainfall in South Korea for each duration and return period: large for short durations, small for durations of about 18 hours or more.
figure.credit: Figure 8 from Lee et al. (2022), Journal of Korea Water Resources Association, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: A 38-year satellite rainfall record gives gridded design rainfall for the whole Korean Peninsula, including North Korea, that agrees with gauge results to within about 20% for durations of 18 hours or longer.
background: Dams, levees and drains are designed for rainfall of a given return period, which is estimated from long rain-gauge records. Many places, including most of North Korea, lack long and reliable gauge data, and interpolating between stations adds uncertainty. Satellite-based reanalysis rainfall offers continuous coverage over decades and could fill this gap.
approach: The authors used PERSIANN-CCS-CDR satellite rainfall (0.04°, 3-hourly) for 1983–2020 over the Korean Peninsula. Annual maxima were adjusted from 3-hour to 1-hour resolution using regressions built from gauge data and then converted to arbitrary-time values with the national conversion factor. A Gumbel distribution fitted by probability-weighted moments gave rainfall quantiles for 12 durations (3–144 h) and return periods from 2 to 500 years. Results were compared with the same analysis at 60 ASOS gauges with complete 38-year records, and South and North Korea were compared.
findings: The 3-hour-to-1-hour adjustment mattered most for short durations: correlation was about 0.95 at 3 h and above 0.99 from 18 h onward.
The satellite location parameter was about 57% higher than the gauge value at 3 h but within 3% for durations of 18 h or more.
Satellite quantiles exceeded gauge quantiles by roughly 70–144% at 3 h, but by less than about 20% at 18 h and longer; for 24 h the mean difference was 1.3% (2-year) to 11.6% (500-year).

North Korean quantiles were smaller: about 84% of South Korean values at 3 h and 70–75% at 144 h; for 24 h, the 2-year value was 149.5 mm in the South versus 110.6 mm in the North, and the 500-year value 496.0 versus 397.4 mm.
relevance: Design rainfall underpins the safety of everyday infrastructure, from storm drains to dams. Satellite-based grids give engineers a consistent first estimate where gauges are missing, which is especially useful for the North Korean side of shared river basins and for future inter-Korean water cooperation.

title: Spatiotemporal analysis of variability in domestic PM10 data using grid based spatial interpolation method
authors: Lee, J., Byun, J., Hwang, S., Jun, C., & Baik, J.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation

figure.caption: Mean (left) and standard deviation (right) of annual mean PM10 over 2001–2019 on a 0.01° grid; concentrations and year-to-year swings were highest around the capital region and in the north.
figure.credit: Figure 10 from Lee et al. (2022), Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation, CC BY-NC 4.0.

tldr: Gridded PM10 maps for 2001–2019 show a clear yearly cycle and a statistically significant fall of about 1 µg/m³ per year, with the capital region remaining the most polluted area.
background: Fine dust is a major health concern in Korea and has been declared a social disaster, prompting national reduction plans. Monitoring stations cluster in cities, so simply averaging them distorts the national picture. Few studies had combined spatial patterns, changing seasonal cycles and long-term trends in one analysis.
approach: Hourly PM10 from 175 to 484 stations per year (AirKorea, 2001–2019) was interpolated onto a 0.01° grid with inverse distance weighting and averaged to daily values. Moving averages and calendar plots showed seasonal patterns, a Morlet wavelet analysis identified periodic behaviour over the whole record and within each year, and seasonal and standard Mann-Kendall tests with Sen's slope quantified trends in monthly and annual means. Annual mean maps and the long-term mean and standard deviation of each grid cell described spatial differences.
findings: PM10 repeats on a very regular one-year cycle, high in winter and spring and low in summer; short (under one month) spring and autumn signals were strong in the 2000s, but the autumn signal weakened over time.
Both tests showed a significant decrease (p < 0.0001): Sen's slope was −1.014 µg/m³ per year for monthly means and −1.071 µg/m³ per year for annual means, from about 60 to 41 µg/m³ over the period.
Concentrations were generally higher in the north than the south, and both the regional differences and the absolute levels shrank over time (the highest grid annual mean was 102.1 µg/m³ in 2001).

Over 2001–2019, the mean and variability were highest near the capital region, with relatively high values also in Gangwon and the industrial east coast of Gyeongsang, and large variability in Jeollanam-do.
relevance: Clear maps and trend numbers help citizens and policymakers see whether fine-dust policies are working and which regions still need attention. The grid-based approach avoids the bias of city-heavy station networks and can be extended to PM2.5 as longer records become available.

title: Evaluation of the storage effect considering possible redevelopment options of the Peace Dam in South Korea
authors: Yoo, C., Shin, H., & Lee, J.*

figure.caption: Simulated releases and reservoir water levels for a 200-year flood under four storage-allocation options (a–d) and four constant release rates R. Lower R values hold back more of the flood peak but raise the water level further.
figure.credit: Figure 6 from Yoo et al. (2020), Water, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: If the Peace Dam near the DMZ were turned into a multi-purpose dam with active gate operation, its flood-control ability could rise from a storage coefficient of 3.9 h to about 22.6 h while also storing water for supply.
background: The Peace Dam was built as a flood-control-only dam to protect Seoul against a possible failure of North Korea's Imnam Dam. It has no gates or reservoir operation: water simply drains through four discharge tunnels. Easing tensions between the two Koreas raised the idea of redeveloping it into a multi-purpose dam, but it was unclear how this would change its ability to control floods.
approach: The authors set up redevelopment scenarios following other large Korean multi-purpose dams: water-conservation to flood-control storage ratios (C/F) of 3, 5, 7 and 9, operated with the Rigid reservoir operation method at constant release rates R of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8. A 200-year design inflow was generated with the NRCS curve-number method and Clark unit hydrograph, with 72 h found to be the critical rainfall duration. The 16 operating cases were simulated, and an exponential nonlinear reservoir model was fitted to each storage–discharge relation to compute a storage coefficient as a single measure of flood-control ability. Cases that pushed the water level above the flood water level (EL. 269.3 m) were treated as unsafe.
findings: The current Peace Dam has a storage coefficient of only 3.9 h, far smaller than other Korean dams with similar storage and basin size.
Release rates of 0.2 and 0.4 raised the water level above the flood water level in every scenario, so they are not safe for this dam; R = 0.6 was safe for C/F = 3 and 5, and R = 0.8 for all ratios.
The storage coefficient depended strongly on the release rate, from about 5.8 h at R = 0.8 to 88.3–89.3 h at R = 0.2.

Considering both flood control and water supply, the most reasonable option was C/F = 3 with R = 0.5, giving a storage coefficient of 22.6 h — more than five times the current value and close to the Chungju Dam (22.5 h) — even with only 25% of total storage set aside for floods.
relevance: The Peace Dam sits on a river shared by North and South Korea, so its future touches flood safety for the Seoul region, water supply and inter-Korean cooperation. The study shows that how a dam is operated can matter as much as its size, and it provides a single, comparable number for weighing redevelopment options. The same procedure can help engineers compare alternatives for other dams.

title: Sensitivity evaluation of the flash flood warning system introduced to ungauged small mountainous basins in Korea
authors: Yoo, C., Lee, J.*, Chang, K., & Yang, D.
tldr: The rainfall threshold used to issue flash-flood warnings in Korea's small mountain basins can shift by roughly ±50% depending on how a few key parameters are estimated, and the river channel width at the warning point is the biggest source of that uncertainty.
background: Flash floods in small, steep mountain valleys rise very quickly and leave little time to react. Korea's flash flood warning system for mountainous regions (FFWS_MR) covers 300 small basins, many of them summer tourist spots, and issues a warning when forecast rainfall exceeds the flash flood guidance (FFG) — the rainfall needed to make the stream reach a danger level. All of these sites are ungauged, so the FFG is built from map- and formula-based estimates, and the system fell out of use partly because it warned too often.
approach: The authors retraced the three steps used to compute the FFG: a threshold flow at the basin outlet (water depth 0.5 m or velocity 3 m/s), the matching effective rainfall from a GIUH-based NRCS unit hydrograph, and the total rainfall via the NRCS curve-number method. For the three most influential parameters — channel width, characteristic flow velocity and curve number — they compared the current system's choices with alternative empirical equations and a revised curve-number classification, giving 18 combinations. These were applied to 30 basins in Gyeonggi Province for 10- and 30-minute rainfall durations, and four pilot basins were field-surveyed to measure the actual channel and basin conditions.
findings: Depending on the channel-width equation used, the threshold flow varied from about −40% to +160% of the current system's value, and the measured thresholds at all four pilot basins were higher than the current ones — suggesting the current FFG is too low, which may explain the overly frequent warnings.
Alternative ways of estimating the characteristic velocity changed the threshold effective rainfall by about −30% to +60% in most basins, and by less than 30% in about half of them.
The revised curve-number classification lowered the threshold total rainfall by up to 46.66% (16.24% on average).
With all three parameters combined, the FFG varied from −54.36% to +52.55% (10-minute duration) and from −49.55% to +65.80% (30-minute duration) relative to the current system.

At the four field-surveyed basins, the FFG built from measured values differed from the current one by only about +5.7% on average, but only because large errors in the individual parameters happened to offset each other; the authors conclude that channel width, and the channel cross-section at the outlet, matters most.
relevance: Flash floods in mountain valleys threaten hikers, campers and small communities, especially during Korea's summer monsoon. A warning threshold that is too low leads to frequent false alarms and people stop trusting the system, while one that is too high misses real danger. The study shows operators where to focus effort — field measurement of the channel at warning points — to make warnings in ungauged basins more reliable.

title: Selection of mother wavelet for bivariate wavelet analysis
authors: Lee, J., Lee, H., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of Korea Water Resources Association

figure.caption: Wavelet coherence between two sine waves with 4- and 8-year periods computed with four mother wavelets; only the Morlet wavelet clearly shows the expected regular co-movement, while Mexican hat and Paul smear the signal across scales.
figure.credit: Figure 10 from Lee et al. (2019), Journal of Korea Water Resources Association, CC BY-NC 3.0.

tldr: Comparing four common mother wavelets on synthetic and real climate-index data shows that the Morlet wavelet is the safest default for analysing how two time series vary together.
background: Bivariate wavelet tools, such as cross wavelet power and wavelet coherence, reveal when and at which periods two series (for example, a climate index and river flow) move together. The result, however, depends on the chosen 'mother wavelet', and the same data can give very different pictures. Clear guidance on this choice for bivariate analysis was lacking.
approach: Four widely used mother wavelets (Bump, Mexican hat, Morlet and Paul) were applied to three synthetic pairs of 672-month series: uniform white noise with a 4-year sine wave, white noise with an 8-year sine wave, and a 4-year with an 8-year sine wave, plus a case with a period change. Cross wavelet power and wavelet coherence were compared with the theoretically expected patterns. The same tools were then applied to monthly Arctic Oscillation (AOI) and Southern Oscillation (SOI) indices for 1961–2016.
findings: Bump and Morlet results matched theoretical expectations best; Mexican hat emphasised short-period variation and Paul long-period variation.
Mexican hat and Paul showed strong 'scale interference' (signals leaking across neighbouring scales) that doubled when the sine period doubled, while Bump and Morlet were barely affected.

Only Morlet and Paul revealed the co-movement between the two sine waves, and Morlet showed it most clearly, especially in wavelet coherence; Morlet was also the only one whose cross power and coherence agreed in the period-change test.
For AOI and SOI, 2–4-year components moved together roughly once every 20 years; with Morlet a strong ~16-year component also appeared, shortening to about 10 years after 1990.
relevance: Wavelet methods are widely used to link climate patterns such as El Niño to rainfall, floods and droughts, including in Korea. Choosing an unsuitable mother wavelet can create or hide relationships, so this study gives students and researchers a practical, evidence-based default.

title: Application of the modified rational formula to time-distributed rainfall events and comparison with the rational formula application
authors: Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation

figure.caption: Peak flow plotted against basin area for 24 artificial basins: (a) results of the modified rational formula, and (b) on log–log axes, the modified rational formula (solid) versus the ordinary rational formula (dashed), which gives lower peaks for smaller basins.
figure.credit: Figure 9 from Lee & Yoo (2019), Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation, CC BY-NC 4.0.

tldr: When a storm's intensity changes over time, the classic rational formula can seriously underestimate peak flow from small basins; slicing the storm into horizontal layers and applying the modified rational formula avoids this.
background: The rational formula is the go-to tool for sizing drains and culverts in small basins because it is so simple, but it assumes rain falls at one steady intensity. Real storms rise and fall, so engineers usually plug in the highest average intensity over the basin's time of concentration. The modified rational formula instead produces a full triangular or trapezoidal hydrograph and can handle uneven rainfall. The two approaches rest on the same idea yet can give different peak flows, and it was not clear how large or why the gap is.
approach: The authors proposed a new way to apply the modified rational formula: instead of cutting the storm hyetograph into vertical time blocks, they split it into stacked horizontal layers, each a block of constant intensity with its own duration, and added up the hydrographs from all layers. This yields simple expressions for peak time and peak flow. They tested it on 24 artificial basins with times of concentration from 1 to 24 hours (areas from about 2 to 8,826 km², back-calculated from a Korean empirical formula) under a symmetric 12-hour, 400 mm design storm distributed with the Yen & Chow model, using a runoff coefficient of 1.0. Results were compared with the rational formula using the average-intensity approach.
findings: The horizontal-layer approach makes peak time and peak flow easy to compute; for a symmetric storm the peak time follows a simple rule based on storm duration and time of concentration.
Example peak flows from the modified rational formula were about 3,195, 13,186 and 25,558 m³/s for basins with 6-, 12- and 18-hour times of concentration.

The largest gap between methods appears when the storm lasts longer than the time of concentration: the average-intensity rational formula then gives clearly lower peaks and risks underestimating floods, especially for small basins.
When the time of concentration exceeds the storm duration and the basin is assumed rectangular, the two methods give practically the same peak flow; this held for other storm durations as well.
relevance: Countless small drainage structures, from road culverts to urban storm sewers, are still designed with the rational formula. This study shows that ignoring how rainfall varies within a storm can make those designs too small, which matters for flood safety in fast-responding Korean urban and mountain catchments. It also offers a simple, practical way to keep the convenience of the rational method while accounting for storm shape.

title: Selecting a mother wavelet for univariate wavelet analysis of time series data
authors: Lee, H., Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of Korea Water Resources Association

figure.caption: Wavelet power of a test signal (a 200-step sine wave plus white noise) analysed with four mother wavelets. Bump shows only a thin, constant band; Morlet and Paul show the 200-step period with realistic spread; Mexican Hat produces a confusing pattern of separate blobs.
figure.credit: Figure 7 from Lee et al. (2019), Journal of Korea Water Resources Association, CC BY-NC 3.0.

tldr: Comparing four common mother wavelets on synthetic signals and two climate indices, the study finds Morlet the most dependable all-round choice for single-series wavelet analysis.
background: Wavelet analysis is widely used in hydrology and climate science to see how cycles in a time series (for example, rainfall or climate indices) strengthen or fade over time, something ordinary spectral analysis cannot show. Every wavelet analysis starts by choosing a 'mother wavelet', the basic wave shape used to scan the data, and this choice changes the result. Yet there is little guidance on how to choose, and earlier studies usually compared only one or two options.
approach: The authors compared four widely used continuous mother wavelets: Bump, Morlet, Paul and Mexican Hat. They first applied them to artificial 1,000-step series made of white noise alone and white noise plus one or two sine waves (periods of 200 and 100 steps), where the 'true' answer is known. They then analysed two real monthly climate indices for 1961–2016: the Arctic Oscillation Index (AOI), which has short memory and behaves close to noise, and the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), which has long memory and clearer cycles.
findings: Bump reproduced the sine-wave periods most cleanly but showed almost no change over time, so its output is essentially the same as a classic spectrum and loses the main benefit of wavelets.
Morlet and Paul captured both the true periods and their non-stationary behaviour, though Paul spread the noise more and blurred the two sine periods together.
Mexican Hat was hard to interpret: for a 200-step sine wave it highlighted the peaks and troughs rather than the period itself.

For the climate indices, Morlet showed a strong 15–20-year AOI cycle around 1980 that weakened later, and an SOI cycle of about 11–12 years that grew stronger after the 1980s; Paul behaved inconsistently, resembling Mexican Hat for these real data.
Overall Morlet was judged the most stable choice, in line with its frequent use in recent wavelet studies.
relevance: Wavelet maps are a common way to link Korean rainfall, droughts and floods to large climate patterns such as El Niño and the Arctic Oscillation. Because the picture depends on the mother wavelet, a poor choice can create or hide cycles. This study gives students and researchers a practical starting point (Morlet) and a reminder to check that the wavelet suits the purpose before drawing conclusions.

title: Bias from rainfall spatial distribution in the application of areal reduction factor
authors: Lee, J., Park, K., & Yoo, C.*

figure.caption: Ratios of peak flows at all sub-basin outlets of the Chungju Dam basin, comparing the three ways of applying the areal reduction factor with each other (a–c) and with the 50 realistic storm patterns, labelled Case 2 (d–f). Points near 1.0 in panel (f) show that Method (3) closely matches the realistic storms.
figure.credit: Figure 10 from Lee et al. (2018), KSCE Journal of Civil Engineering, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

tldr: When converting point design rainfall to basin-wide rainfall, computing the areal reduction factor from the area accumulated up to each design point comes closest to realistic storms, underestimating the basin-outlet peak flow by only about 5%.
background: Design rainfall is derived for a single point, but a storm rarely delivers that intensity over a whole basin at once, so an areal reduction factor (ARF) is used to scale it down. When a basin is split into sub-basins, the ARF can be taken from the whole-basin area (Method 1), from each sub-basin's own area (Method 2), or from the total area upstream of the point where the design flood is needed (Method 3). Korean practice has switched between these methods since 2000, and their bias had never been checked against realistic storms.
approach: The study used the Chungju Dam basin (about 6,648 km², divided into 50 sub-basins) with a 100-year, 24-hour design rainfall of 400.1 mm. The authors generated 50 circular and 50 elliptical (2:1) storm patterns by randomly placing the storm centre and orientation and spreading the ARF outward sub-basin by sub-basin. Runoff was simulated with HEC-HMS using Clark unit-hydrograph and Muskingum routing parameters, after checking that simulated runoff volumes for three observed events were within 2% of observations. Peak flows from the three ARF methods were then compared with the highest peaks from the realistic storm patterns at every sub-basin outlet.
findings: Peak flow depended mostly on where the storm was centred: it was largest with the centre in the upstream part of the basin and smallest near the outlet, while circular and elliptical storms gave almost the same basin-outlet peak (a difference of 0.08%).
Method 2 always gave higher peaks than Method 1, by about 26.8% at the basin outlet (19,703.9 vs 15,544.8 m³/s).
Method 3 matched Method 2 in upstream sub-basins and Method 1 near the basin outlet, and was closest to the peaks from realistic storm patterns.

At the basin outlet, the realistic storms gave a peak of 16,334.3 m³/s — about 5% above Method 3 but about 17% below Method 2 — so Method 3, which is used in current practice, slightly underestimates the design flood.
The authors note the bias depends on basin size and the number of sub-basins and may be under 5% for smaller basins.
relevance: Areal reduction factors appear in almost every design-flood calculation, from drainage channels to dam safety. Applying them the wrong way can make design floods too low at upstream points or too high at the outlet. This study confirms that the method now used in Korea is sound and puts a number on its small remaining bias, helping engineers judge how much safety margin to keep.

title: Storage effect of dam reservoirs: evaluation of three nonlinear reservoir models
authors: Yoo, C.*, Jun, C., & Lee, J.
journal: Water Science and Technology: Water Supply
tldr: Of three nonlinear models for how a reservoir's storage relates to its outflow, only an exponential model gives a usable storage coefficient, and for four Han River dams this coefficient (6.1–42.8 h) is best explained by flood-control volume divided by channel length.
background: A dam reduces floods by temporarily storing part of the flood and releasing it more slowly. This storage effect can be summarised by a storage coefficient, but real reservoirs do not behave linearly, because storage grows much faster than outflow as the water rises. Without a suitable nonlinear model, the only way to judge a dam's flood-control ability has been to simulate its operation for each inflow.
approach: The authors compared three nonlinear storage–outflow relations — power, logarithmic and a newly proposed exponential function — with the linear reservoir model. For each, they solved the continuity equation for an instantaneous inflow to get the reservoir's impulse response, and defined the storage coefficient from the outflow and its rate of change at the inflection point. The models were fitted to storage–outflow curves of the four Han River dams with flood-control capacity (Chungju, Soyanggang, Hwacheon and Hoengseong), using the flood-control zone above the restricted water level. The resulting storage coefficients were then compared with basin and reservoir characteristics.
findings: The logarithmic and power models give a storage coefficient that is zero at the inflection point, so they cannot describe a reservoir's storage effect; only the exponential model gives a realistic value (about 72% higher than the product of its two parameters).
Fitted above the restricted water level, the exponential model had the highest R² of the four models for every dam (0.9927–0.9982).
Storage coefficients ranged from 6.1 h (Hoengseong) and 9.9 h (Hwacheon) to 22.5 h (Chungju) and 42.8 h (Soyanggang).

Flood-control volume alone could not explain these differences — Soyanggang's coefficient was about twice Chungju's despite similar flood-control storage — but flood-control volume divided by channel length showed a strong linear relationship with the storage coefficient.
relevance: Dam operators and planners need a simple, comparable measure of how much a reservoir dampens floods. This work provides that measure and an easy predictor based on flood-control volume and channel length, which the group later used to evaluate redevelopment options for the Peace Dam. It supports better flood protection for communities downstream of Korea's major dams.

title: Parameter estimation of the Muskingum channel flood-routing model in ungauged channel reaches
authors: Yoo, C.*, Lee, J., & Lee, M.
tldr: The parameters of the widely used Muskingum flood-routing model can be set without any flow measurements, using the concentration time and storage coefficient at the two ends of a river reach, and they route floods about as well as parameters fitted to observed data.
background: The Muskingum model is one of the most popular tools for tracking how a flood wave moves and flattens as it travels down a river reach, and it is widely used in Korea. Its two parameters — the storage coefficient K and the weighting factor x — are normally fitted from measured inflow and outflow hydrographs, so the model is hard to apply on reaches without gauges. A way to set the parameters from basin characteristics would extend it to ungauged rivers.
approach: Using hydrograph moments, the authors first showed that K equals the flood's travel time through the reach and that x must lie between 0 and 0.5. Solving the model's continuity equation for an instantaneous inflow, they wrote its impulse response as a weighted mix of a linear reservoir (pure storage) and a Dirac delta function (pure translation). From this they derived simple formulas giving x and K from the concentration time and storage coefficient of the reach, which can be taken as the differences between empirical-formula values at the reach outlet and inlet. The method was tested on a 2004 dam-release experiment from Daecheong Dam, with flows measured 36.39 km and a further 17.27 km downstream in the Geum River.
findings: The impulse response of the Muskingum model is a linear reservoir plus a Dirac delta function weighted by x, so the reservoir's storage coefficient is K(1−x) and depends on both parameters.

Parameters from the proposed method (x = 0.34 for all three reaches) fell within the range estimated graphically from observed data (x = 0.31–0.40), with similar K values (for example 7.15 h vs 6.95 h for the first reach).

Routed hydrographs from both parameter sets closely matched the observed outflow; RMSEs were 10.42 vs 10.02 m³/s, 2.25 vs 1.79 m³/s and 8.89 vs 13.66 m³/s (proposed vs graphical) for the three reaches.
The study also derived the valid range of routing time step for given K and x, and identified the shortest valid step with the reach's concentration time.
relevance: Most river reaches have no flow gauges at both ends, yet flood forecasters still need to know when and how high a flood will arrive downstream. This method lets engineers use a familiar, simple routing model on such reaches using basin information they already have. It is directly useful for flood forecasting and dam-release planning on Korean rivers.

title: Comparative evaluation of hydrological cycle in South and North Korea using a land surface model
authors: Song, S., Lee, J., Cho, E., & Yoo, C.*
tldr: A 30-year land surface model simulation suggests that the water cycles of South and North Korea have drifted apart since the 1990s, consistent with large-scale deforestation in the North.
background: North Korea has suffered heavy losses from floods and droughts, and widespread forest loss after its economic collapse in the 1990s is often blamed for making these disasters worse. Testing this is hard because almost no hydrological data from North Korea are available: streamflow records are lacking and only 27 weather stations report through the WMO. Large-scale land surface models driven by global soil, vegetation and weather data offer a way around this gap.
approach: The authors ran the VIC (Variable Infiltration Capacity) land surface model over the whole Korean Peninsula for 1981–2013, using daily weather from 45 South Korean and 27 North Korean WMO stations. Soil parameters came from the FAO global soil map, reclassified to USDA soil classes. To capture vegetation change, three different land cover maps were used for successive periods: NASA (1981–1992), University of Maryland (1993–2002) and ESA CCI (2003–2013). The parameters were checked against observed runoff in the Chungju Dam and Soyang River basins, and runoff, soil moisture and evapotranspiration were then compared between the two Koreas and between major basins in each.
findings: In the validation basins, simulated runoff ratios (63.6% and 66.0%) were close to observed values (61.4% and 59.0%).
Runoff ratios were about 55–70% in South Korea and 38–56% in North Korea, but year-to-year variation was larger in the North (about 28% versus 15%).
Evapotranspiration ratios were 20–35% in the South and 25–46% in the North, again with wider variation in the North (21% versus 15%).
Average soil moisture was higher in the South (about 34% versus 27%), while its variability was similar in both.

Differences between the two Koreas widened after the 1990s; in the Cheongcheon River basin, where land cover shifted from deciduous forest to grassland, cropland and bare land, the evapotranspiration ratio dropped from up to 45% before 1997 to at most about 25% after 1999.
relevance: Forests act as a sponge that steadies how rain becomes river flow. This study offers rare quantitative evidence of how forest loss may have made North Korea's water cycle more erratic, raising flood and drought risk. It shows how global datasets and models can fill gaps in data-poor regions, and it provides groundwork for shared river management, reforestation and water planning on the Korean Peninsula.

title: Mean-field-bias correction of the rainfall forecasts using backward storm tracking
authors: Na, W., Cho, E., Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation
tldr: Correcting radar rainfall forecasts with a bias factor measured where the storm was two hours earlier, found by tracking the storm backward in time, gives far more realistic forecasts than measuring the factor at the warning site itself.
background: Flash flood warnings in Korea rely on very short-range radar rainfall forecasts (MAPLE), which are adjusted with a G/R ratio: the ratio of rain-gauge rainfall to radar-estimated rainfall. In the current system this ratio is computed at the warning site and then applied to the forecast for that same site. But before a fast-moving convective storm arrives, there is often little rain at the site, so the ratio can be wildly over- or underestimated, or impossible to compute at all.
approach: The authors proposed estimating the G/R ratio where the incoming storm is located now, and then applying it to the forecast for the target area. To find that location, they tracked the storm backward in time using the pattern correlation coefficient between radar rainfall fields (20 × 20 km window, 60 km search radius, assuming a storm speed of about 30 km/h). The method was tested on a 20 × 20 km area around Yangpyeong and Gapyeong in Gyeonggi Province, which includes a designated flash-flood risk zone, for five convective storms in July–August 2016, using 2-hour MAPLE forecasts and five rain gauges.
findings: Backward tracking worked well: for the 16 July storm, the area found two hours earlier had a pattern correlation of 0.84 with the target area and contained 11 rain gauges.
The conventional method gave G/R ratios of 7.4 to 11.2 for three storms and over 100 for the other two, whereas the tracking method gave 2.8 to 5.3 for four storms and 13.1 for the fifth.
After correction, the conventional method produced unrealistic rainfall rates of about 459 and 1,007 mm/h for two storms where gauges recorded about 13 and 12 mm/h.
With the tracking method, corrected rates (6.3–38.2 mm/h) were much closer to the observed 7.5–16.8 mm/h and lay nearer the 1:1 line overall.
relevance: Flash floods in Korean mountain valleys and small streams can strike within an hour, so warnings depend on short-term rainfall forecasts being sensibly corrected. This study shows that following the storm, rather than waiting for rain at the warning site, avoids absurd corrections that could trigger false alarms or hide real danger. It points to a simple, practical upgrade for operational warning systems that protect campers, hikers and riverside communities.

title: Hydrologic regionalization of basin using multivariate statistical analysis: a case study of Gyeonggi-do 30 districts
authors: Ro, Y., Lee, J., Cho, E., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation
tldr: Combining factor, cluster and regression analysis for 30 small flash-flood-prone basins in Gyeonggi-do groups them into three types and identifies stream network ratios as the basin traits most tied to uncertainty in flash flood warning thresholds.
background: Effective flash flood warnings need to reflect local conditions: the same rainfall can cause very different damage depending on a basin's shape, slope, soil and stream network. Grouping basins that behave alike, known as regionalization, helps transfer knowledge to ungauged places and tailor warnings. However, with many basin characteristics to consider, it is hard to group basins sensibly and to tell which characteristics matter most.
approach: The study used 30 small flash-flood risk districts in Gyeonggi-do and nearby Gangwon-do. For each it compiled 11 basin characteristics (field-measured channel width, channel length, area, mean width, shape factor, channel and basin slopes, stream length, area and bifurcation ratios, and curve number) plus the 'range of flash flood warning', the difference between rainfall thresholds from existing and newly built data, used as a measure of warning uncertainty. Factor analysis reduced the characteristics to a few common factors; Ward's hierarchical clustering chose the number of groups and K-means clustering assigned basins to them; multiple regression then linked the factors to the warning range.
findings: After removing weakly related variables, seven characteristics collapsed into three factors explaining 89.6% of the variance: stream network ratios (area, length and bifurcation ratios), basin size (area and mean width), and slope (channel and basin slope).
Three clusters emerged: 20 districts with a warning range below about 410 mm, 9 with 410–1,000 mm, and one district (Jangheung) above 1,000 mm.
Districts in the low-range cluster lay mostly in the north of the study area, while some central and southern districts formed the second cluster.
The stream-ratio factor differed most clearly between clusters, so the area, length and bifurcation ratios were judged the strongest influences on warning uncertainty.
relevance: Korea has hundreds of small mountain valleys where sudden floods endanger visitors and residents, and most of them have no streamflow records. Knowing which basins are alike, and which features drive warning uncertainty, helps agencies set location-specific thresholds and prioritise monitoring. The step-by-step statistical workflow is also a useful template for students learning how to regionalise hydrological data.

title: Markov chain decomposition of monthly rainfall into daily rainfall: evaluation of climate change impact
authors: Yoo, C., Lee, J., & Ro, Y.*

figure.caption: Workflow of the study: from historical daily rainfall and GCM monthly projections to wet/dry transition probabilities, the number of wet days and, finally, the change in rainfall intensity under current and doubled CO2.
figure.credit: Figure 4 from Yoo et al. (2016), Advances in Meteorology, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: For Seoul, only about 30% of the projected change in monthly rainfall under doubled CO2 comes from more or fewer rainy days; the remaining 70% comes from heavier rain on each wet day, which raises flood risk.
background: Climate models (GCMs) give projections of monthly rainfall, but floods and droughts depend on how that rain is spread across days. A change in monthly rainfall can come from more wet days, from more intense rain per wet day, or both. Knowing which dominates matters for judging future flood risk.
approach: The authors assumed that daily wet/dry occurrence follows a first-order Markov chain and used daily rainfall at the Seoul weather station from 1960 to 2014. They regressed the monthly wet-to-wet and dry-to-dry transition probabilities on monthly rainfall amount. Monthly rainfall changes for the doubled-CO2 period (2080–2099, RCP8.5) were taken from 16 CMIP5 GCMs and summarised as average, minimum and maximum after dropping the extremes. These changes gave new transition and stationary probabilities, from which the number of wet days and the required change in rainfall intensity were derived.
findings: Monthly transition probabilities were clearly related to monthly rainfall: wetter months had higher wet-to-wet and lower dry-to-dry probabilities (R² mostly 0.2–0.4 but statistically significant).

For most months the number of wet days changed by less than two days, even where monthly rainfall rose by 70%; only February, March, May, June and December gained more than one wet day under the highest GCM projections.
About 30% of the change in monthly rainfall was explained by the change in the number of wet days and about 70% by the change in rainfall intensity.
The share explained by wet days ranged from about 16% in October to 40% in May, with rainfall intensity making up the rest.
relevance: Many climate-impact studies simply scale rainfall up or down, which hides whether storms will become more frequent or more intense. This study shows that, for Seoul, future rainfall change is mostly about heavier rain on rainy days, which matters more for flash floods and urban drainage. It helps planners in Korea build more realistic future rainfall scenarios for flood design.

title: Performance evaluation of CMIP5 GCMs using CSEOF analysis
authors: Cho, E., Lee, J., & Yoo, C.*
journal: Journal of the Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation
tldr: By comparing the dominant spatial patterns of global annual precipitation, the study ranks ten CMIP5 climate models and finds NorESM1-M and NCAR-CAM5 closest to satellite-gauge observations.
background: Climate change studies depend on global climate models (GCMs), but the many models in the CMIP5 project give noticeably different results, so choosing reliable ones matters. Many evaluations simply compare raw values or basic statistics, which struggle with the complex, non-linear variability of global climate fields. Pattern-based methods that extract the main modes of variability offer a more informative comparison.
approach: The authors took annual precipitation from ten CMIP5 GCMs under the RCP8.5 scenario and compared it with the GPCP v2.2 observed precipitation dataset for 2006–2014, the period when both overlap. They applied cyclostationary empirical orthogonal function (CSEOF) analysis to each dataset to extract its main spatial patterns, matching grid sizes between models and observations. Each model's leading pattern was compared with the observed one using pattern correlation (similarity) and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), summarised on a Taylor diagram.
findings: In every dataset the first CSEOF explained more than 95% of the variance and represents the average spatial layout of annual precipitation, such as heavy rain near the equator and over Southeast Asia.
All ten models had pattern correlations above 0.4 for the first CSEOF; NCAR-CAM5, HadGEM2-ES and NorESM1-M exceeded 0.6, and only NorESM1-M exceeded 0.7.
Seven models had NRMSE below 0.7, with NorESM1-M lowest, followed by BCC-CSM and NCAR-CAM5.
Taking both measures together, NorESM1-M performed best and NCAR-CAM5 second, while CSIRO-Mk3.6.0 had the lowest correlation and the largest error.
relevance: Flood defences, water supply plans and drought strategies increasingly rely on climate model projections, so knowing which models reproduce real rainfall patterns helps avoid building on weak foundations. The study also shows that even the better models capture only around 60–70% of the observed pattern, a reminder to treat projections with care. The pattern-based approach can help Korean researchers pick models for regional climate impact studies.

title: Evaluation of rain garden for infiltration capability and runoff reduction efficiency
authors: Yoo, C., Lee, J.*, Cho, E., Zhu, J. H., & Choi, H.
tldr: A field-tested rain garden in Haman, Korea, soaked up about 90% of ten years of roof runoff in simulations and could offset an impervious area roughly 30 times its own surface.
background: As cities pave over land, rain that once soaked into the soil runs off quickly, raising flood peaks and disturbing the local water balance. Low Impact Development (LID) tackles this at the source, and rain gardens, shallow planted hollows that collect and infiltrate runoff, are one of its cheapest tools. To size them properly, their real infiltration performance needs to be measured and evaluated.
approach: The authors studied a rain garden (about 2 m by 8.5 m, 13.35 m² surface) that receives roof runoff from a building at a relocated military housing site in Haman County. A field test in October 2014 supplied controlled inflows while water levels and pipe outflow were recorded; hydraulic conductivity was estimated with the falling-head method. A simple one-dimensional tank model with Darcy-law infiltration and Manning-equation outflow was built and checked against the observations. It was then run with 10-minute rainfall from a nearby weather station for June–November 2014 and for 2004–2013, using a quarter, half or all of the 208 m² roof, and applied to annual maximum storms to back-calculate SCS curve numbers (CN).
findings: The rain garden's hydraulic conductivity was about 0.0188 m/h (18.84 mm/h), and the model reproduced observed water levels and outflow well (correlations of 0.95 and 0.90).
Over 2004–2013, about 99.9%, 97.6% and 90.4% of inflow infiltrated when a quarter, half or all of the roof drained to the garden; with the full roof, overflow occurred 373 times in ten years.
For the ten annual maximum storms, the back-calculated CN averaged about 50, ranging from 43.1 to 77.7 (one small storm produced no runoff at all).
Since the site's pre-development CN was about 75, the authors estimated that the rain garden can offset an impervious area about 30 times its own surface.
relevance: Rain gardens are increasingly used in Korean cities and new developments to cut flooding and refill groundwater. This study provides rare field-based numbers and a simple rule of thumb for how much roof or pavement one rain garden can handle, helping planners size green infrastructure without wasting land. It shows how a modest, low-cost landscape feature can bring urban runoff closer to natural conditions.
